item.title: Trying to Heal in a Toxic Relationship
item.description:
Relationships

Trying to Heal in a Toxic Relationship

Why understanding the wounds beneath the relationship may matter most.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Knowing why you stay is only the beginning.
  • Staying and leaving both involve pain, and both can be part of healing.
  • Choosing yourself can lead to lasting change.

If you currently find yourself in a relationship where conflict has become the norm, moments of peace are short-lived, and anxiety feels like your baseline, chances are you're exhausted. But you are not alone.

Over the years, I've worked with many clients who come to therapy feeling trapped in a toxic relationship pattern, hoping to find a way off the roller coaster of emotions.

"Things will be great for a while," someone will say. "I'll start thinking everything is okay. But then, boom! Something happens. We have a huge fight, things get heated, and I'll tell myself I'm really 'done.' But after a few days of silence, I start feeling like my whole life is falling apart and that they've really left me. I'm sick to my stomach, like I can't breathe. Then we make up, and the relief is so intense that I almost forget how awful it was… until it happens again. What is wrong with me?"

I've heard so many versions of this cycle. Frustrated and confused, these clients seek therapy ready to work on themselves in the hopes of feeling better and, eventually, leaving the relationship. And even though many want an overnight "aha" moment, we spend a good amount of time first exploring why they stay, as opposed to why they don't leave.

Why Can’t I Just Walk Away?

Not understanding why you feel so powerless to leave can take a tremendous toll on your mental health because it means you're constantly judging yourself for staying despite the harm. That's why answering this question is so important and a crucial part of the healing process.

It's familiar. As painful as the relationship may be, it's a pain you know. You know what to expect. Walking away means facing the unknown: the grief, the loneliness, the uncertainty, and the fear that you may never find another relationship. As strange as it sounds, staying often feels like the safer option.

You feel responsible for them. Maybe they've struggled with their own mental health, or they carry wounds of their own, and something about leaving can feel cruel, like you're abandoning someone who needs you.

You're holding onto hope. Some part of you still believes they'll eventually hear you and understand you, that they'll acknowledge how much they've hurt you and change. You may even believe that if you can just heal yourself enough, maybe you can heal them too.

None of these reasons make you weak. They make you human.

With clients, we agree that understanding why they stay is only the beginning. Eventually, we have to dig beneath the relationship itself to understand how they got there.

But so often, we rarely get the chance to dig because nearly every session is spent processing the latest fight, betrayal, or threat of the relationship ending. Instead of exploring those deeper layers, we focus on regaining some sense of stability, on reminding them that judging themselves for staying only makes everything worse.

After months of therapy sessions, many become discouraged because they don't feel much different and nothing in the relationship has changed.

When Survival Gets in the Way

"Is it even possible to work on yourself and heal while you're in a toxic relationship?" someone once asked me.

It's a fair question.

Technically, yes. You can always work on yourself, regardless of your circumstances. But it's not really about whether you can do the work. It's about understanding what, exactly, you're trying to heal. That distinction is fundamental.

If you experienced ongoing abandonment as a child, emotional neglect, unpredictability, or instability, you may remember those experiences as painful and frightening, because they were.

But the wounds you carried into your relationship aren't the things that happened to you. They may be the beliefs you developed about yourself because of the things that happened. Somewhere along the way, perhaps you stopped believing you mattered. Maybe you began believing you weren't enough, you weren't lovable, or that you would always be abandoned.

If so, the relationship that needs the most healing isn't the one you have with your partner. It's the one you have with yourself.

Trouble is, when you're in a toxic pattern, repairing your inner relationship is incredibly difficult because every argument validates what you already fear is true. Every betrayal seems to confirm it. Every silent treatment reminds you that you're unimportant. Each intense conflict triggers a deep fear of abandonment because some part of you already believes you're not worth much anyway.

By the time the reconciliation comes, the relief is so overwhelming that you're no longer thinking about the deeper issues at play. You're simply wondering, How do I get back to okay again? How do I get back to that place where I haven't been abandoned?

In order to fully heal your relationship with yourself, your nervous system eventually needs enough safety to stop scanning for the next fight, disappointment, or betrayal. But perhaps you're not ready for that step yet. And that's okay. Healing is less about choosing the "right" path and more about understanding what each path asks of you.

The Choice

When someone is on the fence about whether to stay or leave, they often ask themselves the same question: Which option will hurt less? The truth is, if you're trying to find the least painful option, you may spend years waiting for one that doesn't exist.

The reality is that neither path is easy, and neither path is wrong. They simply involve different kinds of pain, and both can be part of your healing.

Choosing to stay often means living with ongoing pain. It means living with a nervous system that's constantly waiting for the next fight, disappointment, or betrayal. Berating yourself for staying only creates another wound on top of the ones you already have. Sometimes the most healing thing you can do is simply tell yourself the truth: I'm not ready yet. That's not giving up. It's being honest.

And this honesty paves a whole new road, one on which you stop judging yourself. You start setting boundaries regardless of the outcome, make time for yourself, or simply acknowledge that it's not okay to be treated the way you've been treated.

When you do these tiny things, you’re sending a different message to yourself: Hey, you do matter. For someone who has spent a lifetime looking for that message from someone else, learning to give it to yourself is healing in and of itself.

Choosing to walk away is painful too. In many ways, it's the harder choice because all the grief, fear, loneliness, and uncertainty you've been trying to avoid show up at once. But walking through that pain is also an act of choosing yourself. It’s not a completely different decision; it's the continuation of one you already started making when you stopped judging yourself: that no matter how difficult it gets, you won't give up.

So, can you work on yourself and heal while you're in a toxic relationship? Yes, absolutely. Because healing doesn't begin the day you leave. It begins the day you stop leaving yourself behind.

item.title: How Fairy Tales Nurture the Creative Self
item.description:
Imagination

How Fairy Tales Nurture the Creative Self

The princess who found her name and other yarns that fuel the creative mind.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Fairy tales may help us face emotions safely
  • Self-enchantment lets us see life as a meaningful story.
  • Magical fantasies may even transform us.

Novelist Dale Kushner has entertained a lifelong fascination with the psyche. In her recent book, Wild Freedom, she notes that we can learn from fairy tales and other ancient stories handed down to us over the centuries. They present a record of universal human challenges—fear, jealousy, abandonment, betrayal—and offer a map to navigating these collective struggles. When all seems lost, we can find ourselves through stories.

Can fairy tales and the unconscious mind help us navigate life's challenges?
For children as well as adults, fairy tales help us make sense of our lives. They speak the language of the unconscious through images, archetypes, and metaphors. They are simultaneously engaging and delightful tales and also representations of psychological truths about ourselves and the world that transcend cultural and racial differences. Fairy tales invite us to face our difficult emotions indirectly and with a sense of safety.

By identifying with characters who confront darkness and emerge transformed, we discover models for resilience, courage, creativity, and hope. Fairy tales remind us that challenges are part of a larger human story and that there is often a silver lining to those challenges if we accept the call to action: unexpected help, insight, transformation.

Do fairy tales offer insight into personal transformation?
Yes. Fairy tales are, fundamentally, transformation stories. The stories we get in fairy tales remind us that our wounds are not only personal but also timeless human dilemmas.

As in fairy tales, so in life—transformation begins with a conflict. Our world is destabilized. We are tested, broken open by adversity, forced to confront aspects of ourselves and others that are unexpected and difficult.

This was true for me. My imagination helped me out of a deep crisis by inspiring me to write an original fairy tale during a time of crisis and despondency. The crisis became an opportunity to re-vision, re-frame, and re-imagine my life’s oath. The fairy tale I wrote, “The Princess Who Found Her Name,” began with an image of a lonely girl staring out a window. This tale is at the center of my recent book—a blend of fairy tale, a memoir-essay, and commentary by Jungian analysts.

Writing the fairy tale and later the essay was a rebirth for me; it became a blueprint for my own psychological growth and self-awareness.

Do fairy tales offer insight into creativity?
Fairy tales catapult the hero or heroine into the territory of the unknown where they must trust their instincts, intuition, and creative powers to defeat adversarial forces. This often involves breaking established rules and becoming a lonely sojourner through the metaphoric dark forest. Fairy tales call us to be courageously creative in the face of uncertainty and to accept help from unexpected sources with humility.

Creativity is a collaboration between our conscious mind and the unconscious. When I write, images and symbols arise spontaneously, without conscious thought, carrying truths I didn’t know I knew.

How can imagination, storytelling, and creativity help people heal from trauma?
As a child dealing with fear and vulnerability, books became my refuge, stories the place where I could imagine another life. In these alternative fantasy lives, I was a clever, resourceful, intelligent girl, capable of overcoming dangers (not realizing I was all those things already).

We are wired to create narratives out of our memories, fantasies, and random ideas. Stories enable us to glean meaning from the chaotic stream of experience. They anchor us in a time-bound world of cause and effect. When we tell a story, we create a distance between ourselves and emotional wounds or deep trauma without directly naming them.

Through storytelling, people can reclaim agency, discover meaning, and create narratives of survival over victimhood. Further, through knowing the stories of others, we quickly realize we are not alone. The lonely princess at the center of “The Princess Who Found Her Name” is every child trapped in a troubled family and longing to find her true home.

How do animal guides bring you personal healing?
For me, animals function as symbolic helpers, messengers from the unconscious, or embodiments of instinctive wisdom. There is a long history of fairy tales featuring magical animals and assisting protagonists when human resources fail. Animal guides can help reconnect us with intuition, resilience, and aspects of ourselves that have been neglected or silenced.

Why is imagination a spiritual practice?
Spiritual practices and imagination are linked aspects of the mind, in which we open ourselves to contemplating the unknown mysteries beyond our rational understanding of the world. Science is one way of knowing the world, and imagination is another way. Spiritual practice is a bridge between these two modes of being.

Imagination opens us up to wonder, awe, possibility, and a connection to something larger than ourselves. Imagination expands our consciousness, allowing us to participate in the ongoing creation of meaning in our lives and in the lives of others. It is the means by which we can empathize with and understand others different from ourselves.

How can the creative self be nurtured when it conflicts with family roles or identity?
To be there for others, we also have to be there for ourselves. Creativity allows us to expand beyond the boxes we or society put ourselves in. I am a parent. I am also a spouse. I am also a professional. I am also a daughter.

Walt Whitman famously wrote in his epic poem, “Song of Myself,” “I am large, I contain multitudes.”

Nurturing the creative self honors our experiences, dreams, desires, and imaginative impulses, challenging established identities and creating new ones. All of that can only enrich life.

How can self-enchantment encourage us to embark on our own journeys of self-discovery?
Self-enchantment is the willingness to view one's life as a meaningful story rather than a collection of isolated events. Fairy tales invite us to see ourselves as protagonists capable of growth, courage, and transformation. By embracing imagination, curiosity, and symbolic thinking, we become more open to unexpected possibilities and hidden dimensions of experience. Self-enchantment encourages us to follow the call toward deeper self-knowledge, trusting that the challenges we encounter may be part of a larger journey toward wholeness. Like the heroes of fairy tales, we learn that the path through uncertainty often leads to wisdom, freedom, and renewal.

We are all heroes.

item.title: Struggling to Get Things Done? 4 Causes, 4 Antidotes
item.description:
Motivation

Struggling to Get Things Done? 4 Causes, 4 Antidotes

Like many problems, struggling to get things done has multiple culprits beneath.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • We all have times when our motivation is sapped and we don't do what we need to do because of stressors.
  • But if it is an ongoing pattern, it's time to look at underlying problems.
  • Common ones are feeling overwhelmed, have underlying mental health issues, or feeling it is not our problem.
  • The key is sorting out the underlying drivers and taking action to put them to rest.
Source: analogicus/pixabay

We’ve all had those days when we didn’t sleep well, are just tired, burned out, or a bit down, and don’t have the energy or motivation to do what we need to do. But if it’s more persistent—you routinely haven’t kept up with paying your bills or even filing your taxes, you're always way behind on your mileage report for work, and you keep putting off cleaning out the garage—maybe it’s time to put it to rest.

You’re not alone—I see many clients with the same complaints: They’re not getting done what they know they need to do. The consequences vary: scolding emails from HR about the mileage report, notices about late payments, the garage is a mess, almost unusable, and your partner is getting fed up. But like most problems, the not-doing isn’t the real problem; it’s the outcome of another problem lurking beneath. Here are the most common culprits and their antidotes:

1. You simply don’t want to do it

Your partner wants the garage cleaned, but if you were alone, you wouldn’t give it a second thought. Ditto for the mileage statement, since it has low impact on your work. What motivates us are our own problems, not someone else’s. Being pushed to solve someone else’s problems can lead to passive-aggressive resistance and resentment. You don’t do it because you don’t want to or don’t see it as a high priority.

Antidote

Start by being honest with yourself about how you really feel, rather than wallowing in procrastination, guilt, and ambivalence. If you’ve been dragging your heels or making excuses, admit to yourself that you don’t want to do it. Next, step back and move from your emotional brain to your rational one. You may not care about the garage, but you care about your partner. You know it’s important to them, and, following your values, you’re willing to step up and do it. Or be assertive, express how you’re feeling, and work together toward a win-win compromise.

Apply the same perspective change to the mileage form: Yes, it’s another bureaucratic pain for you, but you realize someone in HR is simply doing their job, and part of doing your job and supporting your work colleagues is not making their lives difficult.

2. You’re overwhelmed

Just looking at the garage, the pile of bills, or the mileage spreadsheet that HR sends out overwhelms you; you don’t know where to start; it seems insurmountable; it only stirs up anxiety that shuts you down.

Again, feeling overwhelmed is not the problem but a byproduct of others. The common culprits are several. One is a lack of skills: The spreadsheet or the taxes are a nightmare for you because you simply don’t know how to tackle them. Or, perhaps you get flooded with anxiety that makes the bills feel like a mountain rather than a stack of individual papers. Maybe you’re somewhat perfectionistic or sensitive to others, and the garage seems like a Herculean task you will never do well enough. Or, you think that partner, who tends to be critical, will undoubtedly say something that undermines your efforts.

Antidote

Figure out where you’re getting stuck most. If it’s about skills, get help to learn them—contact your IT folks and have them train you on spreadsheets, look up YouTube videos, or, if you can, delegate and find a professional to do your taxes. If it’s anxiety, take a deep breath to help get out of your emotional brain, and plot out baby steps—peel off two bills a day.

And if it’s about your or your partner's perfectionism, talk yourself off the ledge by realizing that the garage is a first-world problem and that any improvement is good enough, or get your partner to support or physically help you.

3. You have underlying emotional problems that are sabotaging your efforts

Here, we’re talking about ongoing, often untreated emotional and mental health issues. If you have AD/HD, for example, your brain struggles with focus and is prone to anxiety and distraction. If you’re depressed, you think, why bother—there’s always something else that will dump on you or make your efforts not good enough. If you have OCD, your compulsions can take over even small tasks and derail your progress. If you have an addiction that pulls you into building your everyday life around getting those dopamine-pleasure-centered hits, you may fail to get necessary things done.

What these have in common is that they make you constantly preoccupied or derailed. You can’t focus because you either hyper-focus or mentally wander off when the task of bill-paying or spreadsheets no longer provides the stimulation you need. Your depression undermines your determination. Your OCD makes your obsessions cloud your priorities because your priorities are about reducing the obsessions with your compulsions. Your addiction makes itself the center of your world, and everything else becomes secondary.

Antidote

These are major issues and are likely undermining vast swathes of your life. Time to tackle them directly with medication, skill training, and therapy.

4. You’re entitled or narcissistic: You do only what you want to do

This is a tough one. We’re talking about primary wiring—personality disorders fueled by genetics or trauma. It’s tough because you don’t usually see it as a problem; it is the way you view the world and others. You believe you’re entitled to do what you do; you blame others for the problems they throw at you. You seem like a bully to others and can feel like a victim when things don’t go your way.

Antidote

Ideally, you step back and recognize what’s yours and what’s not. You try to change your perspective or work through your trauma so it loses its grip. It's doable, but a challenge.

Stepping up

The theme is that "not-doing" can be fueled by myriad underlying problems. The key is to step back, rationally assess how and why you are getting stuck, and then proactively tackle these drivers.

You start by getting support, by learning skills, and by changing how you talk to yourself and how you see the challenges before you.

If not now, when?
